Data wrangling

library(tidyverse)

df_regions <- unzip("regions.zip") |> 
  read_delim(col_names=TRUE,
             delim=",",
             progress=FALSE,
             show_col_types = FALSE,
             locale = readr::locale(encoding = "latin1")) |> 
  mutate(across(c(freehms,hmsacld,hmsfmlsh),                                       ~ifelse(. > 5,NA,.)),        #(1)
         across(c(eqmgmbg,eqpolbg,eqwrkbg,eqpaybg),                                ~ifelse(. > 6,NA,.)),        #(1)
         across(c(trstprl,trstlgl,trstplc,trstplt,trstprt),                        ~ifelse(. > 10,NA,.))) |>    #(1) 
  mutate(across(c(freehms,hmsacld),~ 6 - .))  |>                                                                #(2) 
  group_by(regunit,region) |> 
  mutate(n_resp = n()) |>                                                                                       #(3)
  ungroup() |> 
  pivot_longer(-c(regunit,region,n_resp),names_to = 'var',values_to = 'val') |>                              #(4)
  drop_na() |>                                                                                                  #(5)
  group_by(regunit,region,var,n_resp) |> 
  summarise(mu = mean(val,na.rm=TRUE),
            .groups='drop') |> 
  pivot_wider(names_from = var,values_from = mu)                                                                #(6)  

df_regions_forlater = df_regions
  1. Consider the code above and explain the lines that are indicated with (1) in your own words.

Answer: These lines apply the function mutate, which means to change the variable to three sets of variables. In the first set, the across function was used to iterate through the variables freehms,hmsacld, and hmsfmlsh. It then replaces any value greater than 5 with NA. For the second set of variables, eqmgmbg,eqpolbg,eqwrkbg,eqpaybg, anything greater than 6 is replaced with NA. Finally, in the last set of variables, trstprl,trstlgl,trstplc,trstplt,trstprt, anything greater than 10 is replaced with NA.

  1. Consider the code above and explain the lines that are indicated with (2) in your own words.

Answer: This Line of code reverses the scale for the variables freehms and hmsacld. This way, low scores become high and high scores become low. The purpose of this line is to make the scale for these 2 variables aligned with the scales of all other variables; i.e., 0 is disagree/very bad, and the highest number is agree or very good.

  1. Consider the code above and explain the lines that are indicated with (3) in your own words.

Answer: After grouping the data set by region and region unit, we create a new column - n_resp, that will contain the number of respondents in each group. Thus, for each observation, we will have a variable that indicates the number of respondents from the regions of the observation, including the observation itself.

  1. Consider the code above and explain the lines that are indicated with (4) in your own words.

Answer: Here, we transform our table from a wider table into a longer table, keeping the columns regunit, region, and n_resp, and transforming the rest of the columns into observations in the column named var and the value of each into the variable named val.

  1. Consider the code above and explain the lines that are indicated with (5) in your own words.

Answer: Drops the long-format rows where val is missing — i.e., it removes only the missing measurements per region/var so the later means use available answers.

  1. Consider the code above and explain the lines that are indicated with (6) in your own words.

Answer: After calculating the mean of all the variables for each combination of region unit and region, data was reshapedfrom long format to wide format so that each variable is represented as a column containing the average values of the variables. This makes a table with each row corresponding to a region unit, each column corresponding to a variable, and the cells corresponding to the average scores which makes it easier to compare the variables within regions.

Exploratory data analysis

Data Transformation

data <- data %>%
  mutate(across(c(freehms, hmsacld, hmsfmlsh),
                ~ ifelse(. > 5, NA, .)),
         across(c(eqmgmbg, eqpolbg, eqwrkbg, eqpaybg),
                ~ ifelse(. > 6, NA, .)),
         across(c(trstprl, trstlgl, trstplc, trstplt, trstprt),
                ~ ifelse(. > 10, NA, .)))

# Reversing the scale for attitude variables (ordinal variables)
data <- data %>%
  mutate(across(c(freehms, hmsacld), ~ 6 - .))

## drop all missing values
data <- data %>% 
  drop_na()

sum(is.na(data))   ## to confirm the removal of all missing values
## [1] 0
# ------ Creating Composite Variables from related variables --------------

# Attitudes toward homosexuality ####
data <- data %>%
  mutate(att_homosex = (freehms + hmsacld + hmsfmlsh) / 3)


# Gender equality attitudes 
data <- data %>%
  mutate(gender_equal = (eqmgmbg + eqpolbg + eqwrkbg + eqpaybg) / 4)

# Institutional trust
data <- data %>%
  mutate(instit_trust = (trstprl + trstlgl + trstplc 
                        + trstplt + trstprt) / 5)


# Create a new data frame with the composite variables
data2 <- data %>%
  select(regunit, att_homosex, gender_equal, instit_trust)

# View the first few rows
head(data2)

(2) Correlation Table and Interpretation

## Correlation Matrix
corr_matrix <- data2 %>%
  select(att_homosex, gender_equal, instit_trust) %>%
  cor(use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

corr_matrix
##              att_homosex gender_equal instit_trust
## att_homosex    1.0000000    0.3437720    0.1683586
## gender_equal   0.3437720    1.0000000    0.1525787
## instit_trust   0.1683586    0.1525787    1.0000000

Interpretation: The correlation tables show that there is a moderately positive relationship between attitudes toward homosexuality and gender equality (r = .34), while both have weak positive correlations with institutional trust (r = .17 and r= .15) respectively. This indicate that people who support gender equality also tend to have more positive attitudes toward lesbian and gays. However, trust in institutions has only a small relation with these two attitudes.

Statistical comparison using Independent sample t-test

t_test_result <- t.test(att_homosex ~ regunit, data = data3)
t_test_result
## 
##  Welch Two Sample t-test
## 
## data:  att_homosex by regunit
## t = 34.559, df = 19812, p-value < 2.2e-16
## alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group 2 and group 3 is not equal to 0
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  0.4399543 0.4928606
## sample estimates:
## mean in group 2 mean in group 3 
##        3.959524        3.493116

Interpretation: An independent samples t-test was conducted to compare attitudes towards gays and lesbians in Region Unit 2 and Region Unit 3. Statistical comparison shows that there is a significant difference in attitudes toward gays and lesbians between respondents in Region Unit 2 and region unit 3 as p-value < .001. Respondents in Region Unit 2 (M = 3.96) have more positive attitudes than those in Region Unit 3 (M = 3.49)

Principle component analysis

  1. Perform principle component analysis on the df_regions data. Write the code in chunk ‘pca_chunk’ below.

  2. Discuss and decide how many principal components you wish to retain.

Answer: Based on the results of the scree plot and the eigenvalues, we will be retaining 3 principal components. The Scree Plot shows that 3 PCs explain 82.2% of the variance, and then the plot elbow appears. Additionally, the eigenvalues have 3 PCs with values greater than 1, and then the rest are less than 1. 

  1. Discuss how you would like to label/interpret the retained principle components.

Answer: Based on the biplot and factor loadings, we see the variables in each of the three clusters. In the PC1, we see that 3 variables (freehms, hmsacld, hmsfmls)  that are related to homosexuality are clustered together, therefore we choose to label this cluster: Homosexuality perception and acceptance. For PC2, we see the 4 variables (eqmgmbg, eqpolbg, eqwrkbg, eqpaybg) that ask about attitudes towards gender equality; therefore, we choose to label this cluster: Gender Equality Indicators. Finally, for PC3, we see the variables (trstprl, trstlgl,  trstplc, trstplt, trstprt) clustered, and hence, we label it as: Institutional trust. 

  1. Do you prefer to have the observed variables standardized before running the pca? Why?

Answer:  Yes, because the scales of the variables are not the same. By standardization, we ensure that all variables contribute equally to the analysis. If we don’t standardize, the variables with larger scales will have more effect on the PCA. 

  1. Do you have other suggestions to improve the analysis?

Answer: We ran the analysis with all variables and saw a cluster form with only the variable regunit, but we decided to rerun the analysis without that variable because it’s not meaningful in the context of the research question.

  1. Explain in your own words why pca is an unsupervised machine learning alogorithm.

Answer: Because I did not specify anything that the machine should follow when looking for dimensionality reduction. The algorithm used to reduce dimensionality is only based on internal relationships between variables and had no input from me on how to predict that. Additionally, we do not have labelled data.

 #install.packages('ggrepel')
 #install.packages('factoextra')
 #install.packages('corrplot')
library(factoextra)
 library(ggrepel)
library(corrplot)
 library(haven)

df_regions <- df_regions |> 
  column_to_rownames("region") |> 
  select(!regunit) #drop regunit from the pca

pca <- prcomp(df_regions, scale = TRUE, center = TRUE) #pca

We standardized the observed variables before running the PCA because they were measured on different scales.
Standardization ensures that each variable contributes equally to the analysis.
Without standardization, variables with larger numeric ranges would dominate the principal components, biasing the results.

Additionally, during initial runs, we observed that the variable regunit formed a separate cluster unrelated to the main constructs of interest. Since this variable does not meaningfully contribute to the conceptual focus of the study, it was excluded from the final PCA.

Based on the scree plot and eigenvalues, three principal components (PCs) were retained.

The first three components together explain 82.2% of the total variance, after which the scree plot shows a clear elbow.

Additionally, the first three PCs have eigenvalues greater than 1, while the remaining components fall below 1.

Therefore, retaining 3 PCs captures most of the variance in the data while maintaining interpretability.

Based on the biplot and factor loadings, we can interpret the retained components as follows:

  • PC1: Homosexuality Perception and Acceptance
    This component groups together the variables freehms, hmsacld, and hmsfmls, which relate to attitudes toward homosexuality.
    These variables move in the same direction, representing shared variance in views about acceptance of homosexuality.

    PC2: Gender Equality Indicators
    The variables eqmgmbg, eqpolbg, eqwrkbg, and eqpaybg load highly on this component.
    Together, they measure attitudes toward gender equality across different domains such as politics, work, and pay.

    PC3: Institutional Trust
    The third component includes variables like trstprl, trstlgl, trstplc, trstplt, and trstprt.
    These variables reflect trust in public institutions, such as the legal system, police, and political bodies.

These labels provide meaningful interpretations of each principal component, allowing for easier discussion of social attitudes across regions.

Cluster analysis

  1. Run k-means & hierarchical cluster analysis. Write the code in chunk ‘cluster_chunk’.

  2. Would you prefer to run both analyses on the retained PC’s or on the original set of observed variables? Argue.

Answer:

In this case, I don’t see the big incentive of running the cluster algorithms on PCs, simply because our data doesn’t appear to be high-dimensional (264 regions vs 12 features). I would prefer to run both analyses only on PCs if they wouldn’t converge on the original variables, or there would be clear sings that our data has multicolleniarity issues, noise, etc.

A set of PCs that we choose doesn’t retain all the variance of the original data (and if it does, then it is equivalent to running cluster analyses on observed variables rotated) — so it would be to an extent a simplification. Not only that, each PC has different variance (by definition they are sorted from the highest eigenvalue to the lowest) — cluster algorithms will be giving more influence to higher variance PCs as they (most commonly) use Euclidean distances or a modified version of it, which are sensitive.

Nevertheless, if our set of principal components explains more than 80% variance of the original data, and we expect that most of our cluster separation lies in the higher order components, I don’t see why it would be wrong or unacceptable to run cluster analyses on PCs — it will still be meaningful.

  1. Would you advice to standardize the observed variables before running the cluster algorithms?

Answer:

Yes, absolutely.

In case of K-Means, we are dealing with Euclidean distances between observations and their cluster centriods on each iteration of the algorithm — so in case of different variable scales, the result accuracy would benefit a lot from the standardization, unless we want to end up with variables having different weight and influence in the clustering. But even then, it would still be reasonable to standardize and manually re-scale them.

In case of the hierarchical clustering, most of the linkage approaches also employ Euclidean distances (or other distance measures, but almost all of them are still sensitive to variables being scaled differently) — so the same logic applies, distances are mathematically scale-dependent.

In this case, our variables have different scales (0-10, 0-6, 1-5), so I will standardize them.

  1. Would you advice to standardize the PC’s before running the cluster algorithms?

Answer:

Generally, I would say it depends. But it’s more often “no” than “yes”.

PCA returns the PCs that are, in principle, sorted from the highest eigenvalue to the lowest, meaning that the variance of the first discovered principal component is bound to be bigger than variance of the last one. Thus, depending on how many PCs we decide to retrieve for our dataset, we may choose to standardize the PCs or not to.

In most cases we don’t really need to standardize PCs — yes, the variance, and hence the influence, of each component on the clustering may vary, but if we reduce the dataset to a moderate number of PCs, it would be a solid decision. Not standardizing is just keeping the variance weights from the PCA.

However, if we have reasons to believe that our structure of potential clusters lies in the lower-variance PCs, and we reduce our dataset to a relatively high number of PCs during PCA (let’s say 7, for instance) — in this case, we might want to actually standardize our PCs and force their variance to be equal. This way, PCs with low eigenvalues won’t be overpowered and will still have an influence on the clustering. This is more for when our data is noisy or something else is wrong with it.

  1. How many clusters of regions do you wish to retain? Argue.

Answer:

For both K-means and hierarchical (Ward) I ultimately decided to retain 3 clusters. In fact, performance-wise, the 2 clusters solutions would be the best ones in both of those algorithms, however for the sake of not losing meaningful separations and better interpretability, more clusters were retained. 3-cluster solution was slightly better than 4-cluster solution for the K-means, and for the Ward they were almost equivalent (preference given to 3-cluster solution for better comparability with the K-means result).

  1. Interpret the clusters you retained. Do you have any suggestions for improving the result (e.g. omitting certain features or regions)?

Answer:

K-means (please kindly find the full interpretation below):

  • First cluster (131 region) — high tolerance, pro-equality, high trust;
  • Second cluster (83 regions) — low tolerance, moderate on equality, very low trust;
  • Third cluster (50 regions) — very low tolerance, against equality, low trust.

Hierarchical clustering (Ward) (please kindly find the full interpretation below):

  • First cluster (112 regions) — very low tolerance, against equality, low trust;
  • Second cluster (85 regions) — high tolerance, pro-equality (work parity ~ average), very high trust;
  • Third cluster (67 regions) — high tolerance, pro-equality, low trust.

I would suggest removing ES64, LT021, SK021 regions as in both cases they were the outliers that hindered clusters’ tightness.

K-means

Let’s start with finding the optimal number of clusters.

One way to do it is by looking at the Elbow plot:

d_in <- df_regions %>% 
  select(region, all_of(features)) %>% 
  column_to_rownames("region") 

wss <- list()
km_store <- list()

# Let's try finding SS for 1-15 cluster solutions (30 nstarts each)
for (i in 1:15) {
  set.seed(1000 + i)
  km.out <- kmeans(d_in, centers = i, nstart = 30, iter.max = 100)
  wss[[i]] <- tibble(k = i, ss = km.out$tot.withinss)
  km_store[[as.character(i)]] <- km.out
}

wss <- bind_rows(wss)

# Elbow plot
ggplot(wss, aes(x = k, y = ss)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  xlab("Number of clusters (k)") +
  ylab("Within groups sum of squares")

Interpretation: I would say that k=2, k=3, k=4 could all be considered viable choices (it is a bit ambiguous). However, let’s try to avoid k=2, as even though it might perform better on separation in cluster algorithms, we risk overlooking meaningfully distinct clusters, which can make interpretation harder.

Let’s do a silhouette (example from scikit documentation used as a reference) plot to make a final decision:

# Calculating silhouette for k in range(2, 16)
sil_tbl <- lapply(2:15, function(k){
  set.seed(1000 + k)
  km <- kmeans(d_in, centers = k, nstart = 25, iter.max = 100)
  sil <- silhouette(km$cluster, dist(d_in))
  tibble(k = k, asw = mean(sil[, 3]))
}) %>% bind_rows()

# Average silhouette width
ggplot(sil_tbl, aes(k, asw)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Number of clusters (k)", y = "Average silhouette width")

# Silhouette visualisation for k=3
set.seed(123)
clusterer3 <- kmeans(d_in, centers = 3, nstart = 50)
sil3 <- silhouette(clusterer3$cluster, dist(d_in))
plot(sil3, border = NA, main = paste("Silhouette (k=3)"))

# Silhouette visualisation for k=4
clusterer4 <- kmeans(d_in, centers = 4, nstart = 50)
sil4 <- silhouette(clusterer4$cluster, dist(d_in))
plot(sil4, border = NA, main = paste("Silhouette (k=4)"))

Intepretation: both clusters have “okay” overall ASW (so we can avoid k=2), but k=4 is borderline (0,31). Also, 2 of the k=4 clusters have very low ASWs (0,24 and 0,27), and with k=3 only one cluster has low ASW (0,25). Considering that, let’s proceed with 3 clusters (still keeping 4 clusters option in mind — it only looks slightly worse, not significantly).

# Let's run the K-means algorithm:
set.seed(123)                                   
km.res <- kmeans(d_in, centers = 3, nstart = 50, iter.max = 100)
print(km.res)

Interpretation:

55% of the total variation is explained by the cluster centroids’ differences, which means that we have a moderate separation, and the residual variance (45%) is somewhere within clusters.

From the plot, we can see some outliers: ES64, LT021, SK021.

In the first cluster (131 region, red on the plot), we can see that:

  • ‘freehms’, ‘hmsacld’, ‘hmsfmlsh’ (LGBT tolerance variables) are ≈0,72 to ≈0,75 above average — considerably higher;
  • ‘eqmgmbg’, ‘eqpolbg’, ‘eqwrkbg’, ‘eqpaybg’ (gender equality support variables) are ≈0,30 to +0,54 above average — moderately higher;
  • ‘trstprl’, ‘trstlgl’, ‘trstplc’, ‘trstplt’, ‘trstprt’ (institutional trust variables) are ≈0,64 to ≈0,7 above average — considerably higher.

Conclusion: we can label this cluster as “High tolerance, pro-equality, high trust”.

In the second cluster (83 regions, green on the plot), we can see that:

  • ‘freehms’, ‘hmsacld’, ‘hmsfmlsh’ (LGBT tolerance variables) are ≈0,42 to ≈0,5 below average — moderately lower;
  • ‘eqmgmbg’, ‘eqpolbg’, ‘eqwrkbg’, ‘eqpaybg’ (gender equality support variables) are ≈0,1 to +0,37 above average — slightly higher;
  • ‘trstprl’, ‘trstlgl’, ‘trstplc’, ‘trstplt’, ‘trstprt’ (institutional trust variables) are ≈0,81 to ≈0,97 below average — drastically lower.

Conclusion: we can label this cluster as “Low tolerance, moderate on equality, very low trust”.

In the third cluster (50 regions, blue on the plot), we can see that:

  • ‘freehms’, ‘hmsacld’, ‘hmsfmlsh’ (LGBT tolerance variables) are ≈1,12 to ≈1,19 below average — drastically lower;
  • ‘eqmgmbg’, ‘eqpolbg’, ‘eqwrkbg’, ‘eqpaybg’ (gender equality support variables) are ≈1,39 to ≈1,72 below average — drastically lower;
  • ‘trstprl’, ‘trstlgl’, ‘trstplc’, ‘trstplt’, ‘trstprt’ (institutional trust variables) are ≈0,12 to ≈0,34 below average — moderately lower.

Conclusion: we can label this cluster as “Very low tolerance, against equality, low trust”.

The first and the third cluster are the farthest from each other (5.654200), and the second claster is equally distant from both of them (4.025495 and 4.084233) in euclidean space.

Hierarchical clustering

Let’s now proceed with the hierarchical clustering. Ward’s linkage (and, correspondingly, Euclidean distances as Ward doesn’t digest anything else) were chosen so that we would have a similar logic for clustering as K-means (tries to minimize within-cluster SSE increase with each iteration), but with a hierachical approach (bottom-up and greedy).

# Let's run hierarchical clustering and look at the dendrogram:
dmat   <- dist(d_in, method = "euclidean")
hc_full <- hclust(dmat, method = "ward.D2")

# Dendrogram (with k=3 and k=4 lines)
plot(hc_full, cex = 0.5, main = "Hierarchical clustering (Ward.D2)")
rect.hclust(hc_full, k = 3, border = "royalblue")
rect.hclust(hc_full, k = 4, border = "lightblue")

Interpretation: as we can see from the dendrogram, the best possible solution would actually be the 2 clusters, however, for the reasons mentioned in the “Data preparation for cluster analyses” section, let’s try to avoid it. Between k=3 and k=4 it is a bit unclear which case would be better, so let’s check both of their silhouettes in the further steps.

# 3 clusters silhouette
cl_hier3 <- cutree(hc_full, k = 3)
table(cl_hier3) %>%
  kable("html", caption = "3 clusters silhouette") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = "striped", full_width = F)
3 clusters silhouette
cl_hier3 Freq
1 112
2 85
3 67 
sil_h <- silhouette(cl_hier3, dmat)
plot(sil_h, border = NA, main = "Silhouette (k=3)")

# 4 clusters silhouette 
cl_hier4 <- cutree(hc_full, k = 4)
table(cl_hier4) %>%
  kable("html", caption = "4 clusters silhouette") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = "striped", full_width = F)  %>%
  scroll_box(width = "100%", height = "auto")
4 clusters silhouette
cl_hier4 Freq
1 75
2 85
3 67
4 37 
sil_h <- silhouette(cl_hier4, dmat)
plot(sil_h, border = NA, main = "Silhouette (k=4)")

Interpretation: ASWs for both k=3 and k=4 are almost equal (the 0,01 difference could be considered marginal). In both of those solutions there is a weakest cluster with 0,16 width. Thus both solutions are nearly equivalent in terms of performance.

Let’s give a preference to k=3 solution for the sake of easier comparability with the k-means result:

# Fitting & plotting (on 2-dim)
hc_res3 <- hcut(d_in, k = 3, hc_method = "ward.D2")
fviz_cluster(hc_res3, d_in, ellipse.type = "convex")

Interpretation: we observe the same ouliers in the K-means plot (ES64, SK021, LT021). Removing them would likely improve the fit of both cluster algorithms.

# Attaching hierarchical labels to the table (alongside k-means labels)
cl_map <- tibble(region  = names(cl_hier3), cl_hier = as.integer(cl_hier3))
df_regions_cl <- df_regions_cl %>%
  left_join(cl_map, by = "region")
df_regions_cl %>%
  kable("html", caption = "Table with hierarchical labels") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = "striped", full_width = F) %>%
  scroll_box(height = "400px")

# Cluster profiles for Ward
profile_hier <- df_regions_cl %>%
  group_by(cl_hier) %>%
  summarise(across(all_of(features), mean), .groups = "drop")
profile_hier %>%
  kable("html", caption = "Cluster profiles for Wards") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = "striped", full_width = F) %>%
  scroll_box(width = "100%", height = "auto")
Cluster profiles for Wards
cl_hier freehms hmsacld hmsfmlsh eqmgmbg eqpolbg eqwrkbg eqpaybg trstprl trstlgl trstplc trstplt trstprt
1 -0.9804953 -1.0361077 -0.9811411 -0.7061723 -0.6943805 -0.4476267 -0.7144609 -0.6297056 -0.6594591 -0.6304387 -0.5709824 -0.5373964
2 0.7396077 0.7699510 0.7297537 0.3807804 0.4721810 -0.0119088 0.4839370 1.1165038 1.0467635 0.9149395 1.0598803 1.0913826
3 0.7007285 0.7551974 0.7143095 0.6973875 0.5617199 0.7633797 0.5803729 -0.3638178 -0.2256041 -0.1068765 -0.3901461 -0.4862555

Interpretation:

In the first cluster (112 regions, red on the plot), we can see that:

  • ‘freehms’, ‘hmsacld’, ‘hmsfmlsh’ (LGBT tolerance variables) are ≈0,98 to ≈1,04 below average — drastically lower;
  • ‘eqmgmbg’, ‘eqpolbg’, ‘eqwrkbg’, ‘eqpaybg’ (gender equality support variables) are ≈0,45 to ≈0,71 below average — moderately to drastically lower;
  • ‘trstprl’, ‘trstlgl’, ‘trstplc’, ‘trstplt’, ‘trstprt’ (institutional trust variables) are ≈0,54 to ≈0,66 below average — moderately lower.

Conclusion: we can label this cluster as “Very low tolerance, against equality, low trust”.

In the second cluster (85 regions, green on the plot), we can see that:

  • ‘freehms’, ‘hmsacld’, ‘hmsfmlsh’ (LGBT tolerance variables) are ≈0,74 to ≈0,77 above average — considerably higher;
  • ‘eqmgmbg’, ‘eqpolbg’, ‘eqwrkbg’, ‘eqpaybg’ (gender equality support variables) are ≈0,38 to ≈0,48 above average (with eqwrkbg ≈-0,01 — about average) — moderately higher overall;
  • ‘trstprl’, ‘trstlgl’, ‘trstplc’, ‘trstplt’, ‘trstprt’ (institutional trust variables) are ≈0,91 to ≈1,12 above average — very high.

Conclusion: we can label this cluster as “High tolerance, pro-equality (work parity ~ average), very high trust”.

In the third cluster (67 regions, blue on the plot), we can see that:

  • ‘freehms’, ‘hmsacld’, ‘hmsfmlsh’ (LGBT tolerance variables) are ≈0,70 to ≈0,76 above average — considerably higher;
  • ‘eqmgmbg’, ‘eqpolbg’, ‘eqwrkbg’, ‘eqpaybg’ (gender equality support variables) are ≈0,56 to ≈0,76 above average — high;
  • ‘trstprl’, ‘trstlgl’, ‘trstplc’, ‘trstplt’, ‘trstprt’ (institutional trust variables) are ≈0,11 to ≈0,49 below average — moderately lower.

Conclusion: we can label this cluster as “High tolerance, pro-equality, low trust”.

As we can see, the clusters are a bit different from the K-means result, which makes sense as we used completely different approaches to clustering.

df_solitude <- unzip("solitude.zip") |> 
  read_delim(col_names=TRUE,
             delim=",",
             progress=FALSE,
             show_col_types = FALSE,
             locale = readr::locale(encoding = "latin1"))

Supervised Machine Learning

Data Wrangle

  1. Describe the step and decisions you took when wrangling data. When there is discussion in your group about the right decision, briefly describe the different (opposing) opinions. Code this steps in the ‘wrangle’-chunck.

Answer:

First, we will examine the composition of the df, then, since machine learning does not work with NA values, we will check whether our df contains any. This information will help us in the following steps to decide whether or not we need to impute the missing values.

kable(head(df_solitude), caption = "Orginal DataFrame")
Orginal DataFrame
lonely_obs male agea mnactic domicil hhmmb eduyrs trust_other health netustm aesfdrk hlthhmp hincfel
0 1 65 Retired town 2 12 1.5 3 180 2 0 1
1 0 21 Education bigcity 1 14 1.1 2 570 3 1 2
0 0 53 PaidWork town 3 16 2.3 1 30 3 0 1
1 0 78 Retired bigcity 1 14 1.8 3 0 3 0 2
0 1 64 Retired village 2 12 1.7 2 120 1 0 2
0 0 59 PaidWork village 2 16 2.0 1 120 2 0 1 
sapply(df_solitude, function(x)sum(is.na(x)))
##  lonely_obs        male        agea     mnactic     domicil       hhmmb 
##           0           0           0           0           0           0 
##      eduyrs trust_other      health     netustm     aesfdrk     hlthhmp 
##           0           0           0           0           0           0 
##     hincfel 
##           0

The tables above show us:

1. Some of the features are categorical - which tells us that we shall employ one-hot encoding for those variables (ML algorithms only accept numerical variables and work better with those)

2. While the male variable is already in dumy format, it’s better to turn it into a categorical variable - gender and then after apply a one-hot encoding. This will allow us firstly to better capture the influence of male and female, and to avoid if we ever apply standarization that the variable male - which is numeric, also be standardize. The standarization of this variable will make it loose its meaning.

3. The label - lonely_obs is numeric. Caret only accept factor variables for the label, so we shall mutate this variable here. Also since mutating a variable does not require information about the all dataset, we are safe here regarding any data leakage.

4. The Dataset contains no NAs so we shall not care about imputation in later stages.

Therefore for the next - data wrangle step, will consist of mutate the outcome variable into factor and create a new variable - gender based on the ismale variable.

df_solitude[, "lonely_obs"] <- factor(if_else(df_solitude[, "lonely_obs"] == 1, "yes", "no"), levels = c("yes", "no")) #Turn labels into factor for caret

df_solitude <- df_solitude %>% mutate(sex = (ifelse(male == 1, "male", "female")))
df_solitude[, "male"] <- NULL
kable(head(df_solitude), caption = "Table after transformation")

Distribution of the labels

Since the outcome is a nominal variable, we will use classification models to predict whether a respondent feels lonely or not. In this regard, it is important to note that classification models are sensitive to label distribution. If there is an imbalance in the distribution of categories in the label variable, the model will tend to successfully predict the category with the highest number of occurrences and fail to predict the one with the fewest occurrences.

So that is why it is important to have a look on the outcome variable distribution.

We observe an imbalance in the data that could affect the quality of our model. Approximately 69% of respondents said they did not feel lonely, while only 31% said they did feel lonely. This imbalance could affect the quality of our prediction model.

Data Split

  1. Split, train and assess the supervised machine learning algorithms seen in class and select the best solution. Describe the different steps and decisions you took. When there is discussion in your group about the right decision, briefly describe the different (opposing) opinions. Code this steps in the ‘ML’-chunck.

Answer:

As we have a total of 37,775 data points, we decide to train our model on 80% of the dataset and test its quality on the remaining 20%.

set.seed(42) #Thinking about changing seed 

#To avoid Data Leakages we shall do the pre-processing after splitting

split_1 = initial_split(df_solitude, prop = .8, strata = lonely_obs)
train_val_pool <- training(split_1) 
test_set       <- testing(split_1)  #We don't touch to avoid data leakages

split_2 <- initial_split(train_val_pool, prop = 0.75, strata = lonely_obs)

train_set      <- training(split_2)
validation_set <- testing(split_2)

X_train = dplyr::select(train_set, !lonely_obs)
y_train = train_set$lonely_obs

X_valid = dplyr::select(validation_set, !lonely_obs)
y_valid = validation_set$lonely_obs

Model Train

To predict whether a respondent feels lonely based on the various predictors available to us, we use three classification models: glm, naive bayes, and random forest. We ran all models with five-fold cross-validation. The best model is chosen based on average accuracy and a more in-depth analysis of each model. Since our labels are imbalanced, accuracy alone cannot be a good indicator of the best model.

For the naive bayes model, we tuned the model using three parameters: laplace, usekernel, and adjust. This allows us to obtain the best model.

We wanted to run several random forest models by adjusting the number of three, but due to the time required to do so, we decided to run the model with the default number of trees and save it in order to load and use it in this analysis.

ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 5) #Cross validation for all models

#GLM
myclassifier_logistic = train(x = X_train_scaled1, y = y_train, method = 'glm', family = 'binomial', trControl = ctrl)  

#NB
grid_nb <- expand.grid(laplace   = c(0, 1), usekernel = c(TRUE, FALSE), adjust = c(0.5, 1)) ## grid for NB
myclassifier_nb <-  train(x = X_train_scaled1, y = y_train, method = "naive_bayes", tuneGrid = grid_nb, trControl = ctrl)

#rf

#myclassifier_rf <- train(x = X_train_scaled1, y = y_train, method = "rf", trControl = ctrl)

#saveRDS(myclassifier_rf, file = "myclassifier_rf.rds")
myclassifier_rf <- readRDS('/Users/janebossbaby/Downloads/data analysis 2025/myclassifier_rf.rds')

When considering Accuracy, the Random Forest model performed best, achieving a mean accuracy of 72%. However, as previously noted, accuracy alone is not an adequate performance indicator in the presence of class imbalance. This limitation is reflected in the model’s Cohen’s Kappa value: the Random Forest reaches only 0.21 on average, indicating that just 21% of its correct classifications exceed what would be expected by chance. In comparison, both the GLM and Naive Bayes models achieve slightly higher Kappa values of approximately 0.24 on average, suggesting that—despite lower accuracy—they provide more meaningful predictive power beyond chance agreement.

Before selecting the final model, it is essential to evaluate performance on the validation data and refine the classification threshold to better capture cases of loneliness. Since the primary objective of this study is to identify individuals experiencing loneliness (the positive class), we prioritise Recall. From a prevention and intervention perspective, it is more detrimental to misclassify a lonely individual as not lonely—thereby missing a potentially important intervention—than to incorrectly flag someone as lonely when they are not.

The Generalised Linear Model (GLM) achieved a statistically significant overall accuracy of 71.7%, performing slightly below the Random Forest. However, with class imbalance taken into account, the Kappa value of 0.22 suggests that the GLM provides modest predictive power beyond chance. When focusing on the positive class—individuals reporting loneliness—the model shows limited effectiveness, with a Recall of 27.7%. Although this represents an improvement over the Random Forest, it still indicates that more than two-thirds of lonely individuals are misclassified as not lonely. As such, while the GLM offers a more balanced performance, especially given its higher specificity (91.8%), it remains insufficient for reliable identification of lonely individuals in a preventative context.

Naive Bayes Evaluation

The Naive Bayes model achieved an overall accuracy of 69%, which is slightly lower than both the Random Forest and the GLM. However, given the class imbalance, accuracy is not the primary criterion of interest. The model attains a Kappa value of 0.22, similar to the GLM, indicating that it offers the greatest improvement over chance-level classification compare to the Random Forest. Most importantly, Naive Bayes performs comparatively better in identifying individuals experiencing loneliness, with a Recall of 38.8%. Although still modest, this represents a substantial improvement relative to the Random Forest (21%) and the GLM (28%). This means that Naive Bayes succeeds in detecting nearly four out of ten lonely individuals. While its specificity (82%) is lower than that of the other models—reflecting a higher rate of false positives—this trade-off is more acceptable in a prevention-oriented context, where failing to identify lonely individuals carries greater risk than incorrectly flagging non-lonely individuals.

We therefore decided to tune the Naive Bayes prediction threshold to see if this would allow us to increase recall without significantly affecting the accuracy of our model.

Model Tuning

# p_yes <- predict(myclassifier_nb, X_test_scaled1, type="prob")[,"yes"]
# ypred01 <- factor(ifelse(p_yes>=0.1,"yes","no"), levels=c("yes","no"))

 library(pROC)


p_yes <- predict(myclassifier_nb, newdata = X_valid_scaled1, type = "prob")[, "yes"]

my_roc_curve <- roc(response = y_valid, predictor = p_yes, levels = c("yes","no"))
# my_roc_curve
# plot(my_roc_curve)

optimal_th = my_roc_curve$threshold[which.max(my_roc_curve$sensitivities + my_roc_curve$specificities)] 
optimal_th
## [1] 0.2006151
roc_2 = roc(y_valid ~ p_yes, plot=T, print.auc=T,
          print.thres="best", print.thres.patterns="Best threshold: %1.2f")

target_coords <- coords(
  my_roc_curve,
  x = "best",
  input = "threshold",
  ret = c("threshold", "sensitivity", "specificity", "ppv") # 'ppv' is Precision
)

target_coords %>%
  kable("html") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = "striped", full_width = F)
threshold sensitivity specificity ppv
threshold 0.2006151 0.6723806 0.5645366 0.7723451

The ROC analysis yielded an AUC of 0.68, indicating a modest level of discriminatory ability. This means that the model can correctly distinguish between individuals who report loneliness and those who do not approximately 68% of the time, which is above chance level but still reflects limited predictive performance. The optimal classification threshold identified from the ROC curve was 0.139, which maximised the balance between sensitivity (0.639) and specificity (0.626). This threshold was therefore selected for further tuning and evaluation to improve the model’s capacity to detect individuals experiencing loneliness.

pred_optimal = ifelse(p_yes>optimal_th , "no", "yes")
# pred_optimal = ifelse(y_pred4>optimal, "user", "non-user") 
confmat_opt = table(y_valid, pred_optimal)

#recall
recall <- diag(confmat_opt)/rowSums(confmat_opt)
recall %>%
  kable("html", col.names = "Recall Score") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = "striped", full_width = F)

no 0.6723806

  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = "striped", full_width = F)
Precision Score

Using the threshold derived from the ROC curve (~0.2), we are able to identify approximately 56% of people who are truly lonely and correctly identify 67% of people who are not lonely. The model has an accuracy rate of 44% when predicting loneliness (many false positive) and 77% when predicting the absence of loneliness. After adjustment, the model performs significantly better than the previous one.

Model Selection

Next, we use the best model with the optimal threshold to make a final decision regarding the final model. We used the same pre-processing for the test variables as we did for the training and validation variables.

X_test = dplyr::select(test_set, !lonely_obs)
y_test = test_set$lonely_obs

pp_model <- preProcess(X_train, method = c("center", "scale"))
X_test_scaled <- predict(pp_model, newdata = X_test)
X_test_scaled1 <- fastDummies::dummy_columns(X_test_scaled, remove_selected_columns = TRUE)



p_yes_test <- predict(myclassifier_nb, newdata =X_test_scaled1, type = "prob")[, "yes"]

pred_fac <- factor(ifelse(p_yes_test > 0.2, "yes","no"), levels=c("yes","no"))
confusionMatrix(pred_fac, y_test, positive = "yes")

The model achieves an accuracy of 65% with a recall of 56%. This result closely matches our evaluation model, indicating that there is no overfitting of the model. Therefore, the best model for our study is the naive Bayesian model with a prediction threshold of 20% for people who feel lonely.

  1. Would you advice social organisations to use your model? Why (not)? What could be improved? What would your next steps be?

Answer:

Advice on Current Use: Not Recommended

We would strongly advise against using this model in its current state as a standalone screening tool. The risks significantly outweigh the benefits.

  • High Risk of False Negatives: The model’s 56% recall means it fails to identify 44% of individuals who are genuinely lonely. In a social support context, this false-negative rate is unacceptably high. It translates to leaving a large portion of the target vulnerable population without the help they need.

  • Inefficient Resource Allocation: The trade-off for our recall rate was low precision. This means the model produces a high number of false positives—flagging individuals as “lonely” when they are not. For a social organisation with limited resources, this would lead to time and money being wasted on unnecessary interventions, diluting the support available for those who truly need it.

The only potential application would be as a minor supportive tool to complement existing professional knowledge. For example, it could provide one of several data points to help practitioners prioritise outreach, but it should never be the deciding factor.

What Could Be Improved?

The model’s primary weakness stems from the data it was trained on.

  1. Address the Data Imbalance: The most critical issue is the imbalanced dataset. The model’s poor recall is likely a direct result of having an insufficient number of “lonely” respondents. It learned to be accurate by defaulting to the majority “not lonely” class. The best solution is to collect more data from lonely individuals to create a balanced sample.

  2. Explore Algorithmic Techniques: If collecting new data is not feasible, we could use algorithmic sampling techniques. Methods like SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique) could be used to create synthetic examples of the “lonely” class, providing the model with more balanced data to learn from.

  3. Re-evaluate Predictors: Even with a balanced sample, our current predictors may not be the best. We must re-evaluate if the selected variables are truly the strongest indicators of loneliness.

What Would Your Next Steps Be?

Given the model’s current performance, a pivot in strategy is required. Here are my recommended next steps:

  1. Halt Predictive Deployment: Immediately pause any consideration of using this model for prediction.

  2. Pivot to Explanatory Analysis: Instead of predicting, we should first use the model to understand. My next step would be to conduct a feature importance analysis. This will reveal which variables in our current data have the strongest statistical impact on loneliness.

  3. Deliver Actionable Insights: We can provide the organisation with these findings now. Knowing the top 3-5 factors most associated with loneliness can help them refine their current, human-led outreach and support strategies, even without a predictive model.

  4. Develop a New Data Strategy: Based on these insights, we can build a much more informed plan to either gather new, balanced data or apply the right algorithmic techniques.

  5. Rebuild and Re-evaluate: Only after addressing the core data problem would we attempt to build and validate a new predictive model, with a clear focus on achieving a much higher, safer recall rate.
